steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Permanent joints cannot be disassembled without damage: welding, brazing, soft soldering, riveting and adhesive bonding.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Temporary joints can be repeatedly assembled and disassembled: bolts, nuts, screws, clips and captive fasteners.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Welding fuses metals together by melting the parent material (and usually a filler rod); MIG, TIG and MMA are common arc welding processes.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Brazing joins metals by melting a filler (brass alloy, above 450 degrees C) that flows by capillary action between closely fitting parts.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Classify joints as permanent or temporary first — this is almost always required in exam answers. When comparing welding processes, focus on: precision (TIG), speed (MIG), and material suitability. The temperature distinction matters: brazing above 450 degrees C, soft soldering below 450 degrees C. HAZ questions are common — explain that properties change due to thermal cycling, not direct melting. Always justify joint choice by linking it to the application requirement (disassembly, strength, materials).
